summary: Christian pilgrimage is the devotional practice of journeying to holy sites, above all Jerusalem and the Holy Land, Rome, and (from the medieval period) Santiago de Compostela and the Marian and saints' shrines, to pray, to venerate relics, and to seek grace or healing at places sanctified by biblical events, the lives of the saints, or the presence of relics. It is a widespread and historically continuous practice rather than an obligation of the faith: no scriptural command requires it, and the Reformers criticized it. Its development is documented from the earliest visits to the biblical sites of Palestine (attested in the fourth-century pilgrim accounts, including the diary of Egeria) through the flourishing of medieval pilgrimage and its cult of relics and shrines.
description:
Christian pilgrimage is the practice of travelling to a holy place for devotional ends: to pray at a site made holy by a biblical event, to venerate the relics of a saint, to fulfil a vow, to do penance, or to seek healing or grace. Unlike the hajj in Islam, it is not a duty binding on every believer; it is a widespread and historically continuous devotion, undertaken by choice and taking many forms, from the great long-distance journeys to local visits to a nearby shrine.

The principal destinations are Jerusalem and the Holy Land, the sites of the life, death, and resurrection of Jesus; Rome, with the tombs of the apostles Peter and Paul; and, from the ninth century, Santiago de Compostela in Spain, the reputed burial place of the apostle James, reached by the network of pilgrim roads known as the Camino. To these were added innumerable shrines of saints and relics across Europe (Canterbury, with the tomb of Thomas Becket; Walsingham; Cologne) and, especially in the modern period, Marian apparition sites such as Lourdes, Fatima, and Guadalupe.

Historically, pilgrimage to the biblical sites of Palestine is attested from the fourth century, after the conversion of Constantine and the building of churches at the holy places. The diary of Egeria (Etheria), a late-fourth-century woman, most likely a nun, who travelled through Egypt, Sinai, and the Holy Land, records the practice in detail: on arriving at each holy place the appropriate passage of scripture was read on the spot and prayer was made, so that, in her account, at Mount Sinai the custom was that 'prayer should be made by those who arrive here' when the mountain first comes into view, and at each site 'the lection was read from the books of Moses' and a psalm said before the party went on. Medieval pilgrimage grew into a mass phenomenon, bound up with the cult of relics and saints, the granting of indulgences, the growth of shrine economies (hostels, guides, badges, and the trade in relics and souvenirs), and a substantial travel literature. Diana Webb and other historians treat this development and its social, economic, and cultural dimensions.

Pilgrimage has also been the object of theological ambivalence within Christianity, and this is recorded here as attributed position, not adjudicated. The Protestant Reformers criticized it: they attacked the abuses attached to relics, indulgences, and shrine cults, and denied that grace was to be sought by travelling to particular holy places rather than through faith, so that pilgrimage was sharply curtailed in the Reformed and much of the Lutheran world. Within the traditions that retained it, pilgrimage continued as a valued devotion, and a strand of Christian reflection, ancient and modern, reads the whole Christian life as itself a pilgrimage toward the heavenly Jerusalem, a metaphor distinct from the physical practice. Sociologically, pilgrimage is a lived devotional practice with a marked social and economic dimension, gathering people across ranks around holy places and sustaining the institutions, routes, and economies that served them. This entry describes the practice and its history and reports the Reformation critique and the differing valuations of pilgrimage as the attributed positions of the traditions concerned.
editorial_notes:
This entry describes Christian pilgrimage as a lived devotional practice and reports its theological ambivalence, above all the Protestant Reformers' critique of relics, indulgences, shrine cults, and the seeking of grace at holy places, strictly as attributed positions, per neutrality principles #1, #2, and #4. The editor does not adjudicate whether pilgrimage is meritorious or the Reformers' critique justified. The entry is explicit that pilgrimage is a widespread devotion and not an obligation of the faith (there is no scriptural command requiring it), which distinguishes it from the hajj and is load-bearing for the cross-tradition comparisons.

Sourcing triangulates the three lenses per neutrality #8 as adapted for Christianity. (a) Academic historian: Diana Webb, Medieval European Pilgrimage, c.700-c.1500 (Palgrave Macmillan, 2002), a scholarly survey of the history, geography, and cultural legacy of medieval Christian pilgrimage. (b) The primary corpus, read directly and open: the Pilgrimage of Egeria (Etheria), the late-fourth-century pilgrim diary, in the public-domain McClure and Feltoe translation (SPCK, 1919) hosted openly at CCEL. (c) A contemporary Christian theologian on-topic: Craig G. Bartholomew, Where Mortals Dwell: A Christian View of Place for Today (Baker Academic, 2011), which treats pilgrimage and holy place theologically. No encyclopedias, no Wikipedia, no tertiary sources.

CONFIDENCE HONESTY. The primary source (Egeria, McClure-Feltoe translation) was read directly at CCEL (2026-07-26); the load-bearing detail was confirmed verbatim: that on arriving at each holy place 'the lection was read' (at Sinai, 'from the books of Moses') and 'prayer was made' before the party moved on, and that at the approach to Mount Sinai 'the custom is that prayer should be made by those who arrive here, when from this place the mount of God is first seen.' On the strength of that direct reading the Egeria source is rated high for what was read. The entry as a whole, however, is set at status 'reviewed', not 'verified': Egeria attests the fourth-century practice at the holy places, but there is no obligatory scriptural basis for pilgrimage (unlike the hajj or the Torah-commanded festival pilgrimage), and the entry's larger historical and theological claims (the medieval flourishing, the shrine economies, the Reformation critique) rest on the historical scholarship (Webb) and the contemporary theologian (Bartholomew), which were verified to exist and be on-topic but not read line-by-line, so they are rated medium. The honest ceiling for this entry, given that it rests on historical scholarship rather than a body of read-verbatim primary texts adjudicating a doctrine, is 'reviewed'.

Relation targets present in the dataset: indulgences. The compares_with targets hajj (Islam) and aliyah-la-regel (Judaism) exist in the dataset. Each compares_with note states the shared question (pilgrimage as sacred practice) and the difference (Christian pilgrimage is non-obligatory devotion, unlike the obligatory hajj pillar or the Torah-commanded festival pilgrimage), and ranks nothing, per neutrality #10.

relations.note: Medieval pilgrimage was closely bound up with the granting of indulgences attached to visiting particular shrines and relics; this connection, and the abuses attached to it, were among the objects of the Reformation critique. Recorded historically, not endorsed.

Shared question: journeying to a sacred place as a religious practice. Difference: the hajj is one of the five pillars of Islam, an obligation binding once in a lifetime on every Muslim who is able, performed at a fixed place (Mecca) and time with a prescribed set of rites, whereas Christian pilgrimage is a non-obligatory devotion, undertaken by choice, to a range of holy places, with no single fixed rite and no scriptural command requiring it. The comparison states the shared theme and the difference in obligation; it ranks nothing and equates nothing. Target (hajj) exists in the dataset.

Shared question: pilgrimage to a holy place as sacred practice. Difference: aliyah la-regel, the festival pilgrimage to the Temple in Jerusalem on the three pilgrimage festivals (Pesach, Shavuot, Sukkot), is commanded in the Torah for the period of the Temple, whereas Christian pilgrimage is a non-obligatory devotion without a scriptural command and directed at a plurality of holy sites. The comparison states the shared theme and the difference in obligation and object; it ranks nothing and equates nothing. Target (aliyah-la-regel) exists in the dataset.

historical_period.note: Pilgrimage to the biblical sites of Palestine is attested from the fourth century, after the conversion of Constantine and the building of churches at the holy places (the diary of Egeria dates to c. 381-384). Rome and, from the ninth century, Santiago de Compostela became major destinations; medieval pilgrimage flourished through roughly the fifteenth century, when the Reformation critique curtailed the practice in the Protestant world. Pilgrimage remains a living Christian devotion (Lourdes, Fatima, the Camino), so no end date is asserted; the start marks the fourth-century emergence of documented pilgrimage to the holy places.

sources.citation: The Pilgrimage of Egeria (Etheria), late fourth century, translated by M. L. McClure and C. L. Feltoe (London: Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge, 1919). The travel diary of a late-fourth-century woman, most likely a nun, who journeyed through Egypt, Sinai, and the Holy Land visiting the biblical sites. Primary text; read directly. Load-bearing detail confirmed verbatim: at each holy place 'the lection was read' (at Sinai 'from the books of Moses') and 'prayer was made' before the party moved on; at the approach to Mount Sinai the guides said that 'the custom is that prayer should be made by those who arrive here, when from this place the mount of God is first seen.' The primary-corpus lens for the earliest detailed account of Christian pilgrimage to the holy places, showing scripture read on the spot and prayer made at each site.
sources.license: Public domain (the McClure-Feltoe 1919 translation is out of copyright). Read directly at the Christian Classics Ethereal Library (CCEL) (2026-07-26); the cited passages confirmed verbatim.

sources.citation: Webb, Diana. Medieval European Pilgrimage, c.700-c.1500. European Culture and Society series. Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2002. A scholarly survey of medieval Christian pilgrimage: its major destinations (Jerusalem, Rome, Santiago) and local shrines, its geography, the cult of relics and saints, and its cultural and social legacy between the conversion of Constantine and the Reformation. Diana Webb was Senior Lecturer in History at King's College London. The academic-historian lens.

sources.citation: Bartholomew, Craig G. Where Mortals Dwell: A Christian View of Place for Today. Grand Rapids, MI: Baker Academic, 2011. A contemporary Christian theological study of place, closing with a practical section that applies its account of Christian 'implacement' to the city, the home, the church, memorial, and pilgrimage; the author also co-edited Explorations in a Christian Theology of Pilgrimage (Ashgate). The contemporary-theologian lens for a theological treatment of pilgrimage and holy place.
